changelog.change: Added a refractory-VF section — vector change vs DSED, DOSE-VF results, technique specifics (sequential not simultaneous), and the honest evidence framing (single early-stopped trial, guidelines grade low certainty).
Initial entry — original card built from public-domain clinical science, not AHA's diagrams or wording.

summary: Original algorithm card describing the same clinical steps as AHA ACLS (2025 refresh). Not AHA's copyrighted expression — see build note.

items: Continuous high-quality CPR: rate 100-120/min, depth ≥ 2 in, full recoil, interruptions < 10 s
Rhythm check every 2 minutes; switch compressors every 2-5 minutes
IV access is now preferred over IO for drug delivery (IO acceptable when IV isn't feasible)

body.text: Defibrillate → resume CPR immediately → epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3-5 min → after the 3rd shock, amiodarone 300 mg (then 150 mg) OR lidocaine 1-1.5 mg/kg for refractory VF/pVT.

About a quarter of VF arrests are still in VF after three standard shocks. Survival falls with each additional shock (registry: ~29% at 1–3 shocks → ~12% at 4–10 → ~5% beyond 10). First: optimise the basics — compression quality, pad placement and skin contact, maximal energy, and treat reversible causes (much 'refractory' VF is actually RECURRENT VF re-fibrillating after transient termination). Two escalation options:

items: Vector change: move the pads from anterolateral to anterior–posterior, changing the current pathway through the myocardium.

Double sequential external defibrillation (DSED): a second defibrillator with pads in the second (AP) vector; deliver the two shocks in rapid SEQUENCE — one operator presses, then the other immediately after — NOT simultaneously (simultaneous discharge can damage the devices).

body.text: DOSE-VF (NEJM 2022, cluster-randomised crossover, Ontario): survival to discharge 13.3% standard vs 21.7% vector change vs 30.4% DSED; DSED was the only strategy to also significantly improve good neurologic outcome (27.4% vs 11.2%). Caveats: a single trial, stopped early at 405 of a planned 930 patients (early stopping overestimates effect), the vector-change survival finding has a fragility index of 1, and the per-protocol analysis lost significance. ILCOR / AHA / ANZCOR grade the evidence low-to-very-low certainty and do NOT recommend DSED or vector change for routine use — treat them as a reasonable option for genuine refractory VF when standard shocks have failed, not as standard care.
Continue CPR → epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 min → aggressively treat reversible causes.

Hypovolemia · Hypoxia · Hydrogen ion (acidosis) · Hypo-/hyperkalemia · Hypothermia · Tension pneumothorax · Tamponade (cardiac) · Toxins · Thrombosis (pulmonary) · Thrombosis (coronary). (The pediatric list adds Hypoglycemia as its own item — see the Peds Module.)

items: One unified Chain of Survival (adult + pediatric, IHCA + OHCA)
Vasopressin removed from the standard drug sequence — pull it from code carts
Naloxone explicitly in the BLS algorithm for suspected opioid-associated arrest
Post-arrest temperature control for ≥ 36 h in adults not following commands
Infant compressions: two-finger technique eliminated (heel of one hand or two-thumb encircling)
DSED / vector-change defibrillation still not recommended for routine use

body.text: Post-ROSC care is a continuation of resuscitation: targeted temperature management, avoid hypotension, meet ventilation/oxygenation targets, early cath lab if a cardiac cause is suspected.
